### Independent corroboration from a wire-level vantage point, plus a continuation experiment

I run a small local proxy ([codexcomp](https://github.com/dzshzx/codexcomp), MIT) between Codex CLI and the ChatGPT backend that inspects `reasoning_tokens` of every model round in real time — so this is live wire-level observation, not post-hoc telemetry. Sharing 2 days of data as additional evidence, plus a continuation experiment that telemetry alone can't show.

**Environment**: Codex CLI 0.142.5 · `gpt-5.5` · `model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh"` · ChatGPT backend (`chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`) · single user, real coding workload · 2026-07-04 → 2026-07-06 (UTC+8).

#### 1. Boundary clustering reproduces — and extends beyond 1552

| Metric | Value |
| --- | ---: |
| Model rounds observed | 275 |
| Completed requests | 223 |
| Rounds landing exactly on `518·n − 2` | 47 (17.1% of all rounds) |
| Rounds with `reasoning_tokens ≥ 516` | 73 |
| **Exact-boundary / ≥516 ratio** | **64.4%** |

Exact hits by boundary: `516` ×41, `1034` ×4, `2070` (= 518·4−2) ×1, `2588` (= 518·5−2) ×1. The family extends at least to n=5, beyond the 516/1034/1552 trio in the OP.

The OP's aggregate found 44.0% of gpt-5.5 responses with ≥516 reasoning landing exactly on 516 (vs 1.3% for other models). My xhigh-only sample is even more skewed: 64% of such rounds land exactly on a `518n−2` value. Natural stopping should not produce fixed-point clustering like this.

#### 2. Continuation experiment: the model resumes when handed its own reasoning back

The proxy doesn't just observe. When a round ends exactly on the fingerprint, it discards the tentative output, replays that round's reasoning items (including encrypted reasoning) with a continue nudge, and folds the rounds into a single downstream response. Over the same window:

- 36 of 223 completed requests (16.1%) triggered at least one continuation.
- In 21/36, the model **kept reasoning** after replay — median +188 reasoning tokens, max +1,999 (a request truncated at 516 went on to reason ~4.9× its truncated total before answering).
- 5 requests were re-truncated **exactly on a boundary again** on the continuation round (e.g. 516 → 516 → clean); one request needed 3 continuations.
- In 15/36 the continuation produced no further reasoning (the model went straight to output) — plausibly benign near-boundary stops.
- All 36 folded requests then finished with `status=completed`, `stop=natural`.

The repeated re-truncation at exactly the same fixed boundary after an explicit continue is the part I find hardest to square with anything other than a server-side thresholded reasoning budget.

**Caveats**: single user, one machine, 2-day window, `xhigh` effort only, small n. Log format and methodology are in the repo README; happy to share sanitized raw fold logs if useful.

### Follow-up: 80-run controlled A/B — gpt-5.4 vs gpt-5.5 × 4 efforts × mitigation on/off

Following up on [my earlier comment](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30364#issuecomment-4891715438) with a controlled experiment instead of passive traffic: **2 models (gpt-5.4, gpt-5.5) × 4 reasoning efforts (low/medium/high/xhigh) × continuation-mitigation on/off × 5 runs = 80 runs**, all on the same fixed prompt.

**Method**
- Fixed task: a 4-house zebra-style logic puzzle (13 clues, brute-force-verified unique solution), "reply with only the name" → machine-gradable correctness. Pure reasoning, no tools, single model round per run.
- `codex exec --json --ephemeral` (CLI 0.142.5, read-only sandbox), ChatGPT backend, one account, one machine, all 80 runs inside one ~26-minute window (2026-07-06), conditions interleaved rep-by-rep to avoid time-of-day bias. All 80 runs exited cleanly.
- **off** = straight to the backend (`openai_base_url` override); reasoning tokens read from `turn.completed` usage. **on** = through [codexcomp](https://github.com/dzshzx/codexcomp), which detects a round ending at exactly `518·n − 2` reasoning tokens and replays the round's reasoning (incl. encrypted items) with a continue nudge; per-round data from the proxy's logs. Bypass isolation was verified (zero proxy traffic during off runs).

**Results** (each cell = 5 runs; "516 events" = runs where a model round ended at exactly 516 reasoning tokens)

| gpt-5.4 | xhigh | on | **1/5** | 516+76, 634, 839, 957, 963 | 5/5 |
| gpt-5.5 | low | off | 0/5 | 217–276 | 5/5 |
| gpt-5.5 | low | on | 0/5 | 196–266 | 5/5 |

| gpt-5.5 | xhigh | off | **4/5** | 450, **516, 516, 516, 516** | **4/5** |
| gpt-5.5 | xhigh | on | **1/5** | 379, 471, 478, 516+0, 791 | 5/5 |

(`516+k` = round truncated at exactly 516, continuation produced k further reasoning tokens.)

**Observations**

1. **The fixed point reproduces under controlled conditions.** 11 of 80 runs (14%) had a round end at exactly 516. In final usage, 516 appeared 8 times; no other value appeared more than twice across all 80 runs. No run ever landed on 515 or 517.
2. **It is effort-gated, not effort-monotonic.** Hits concentrate where the task's natural reasoning length approaches 516 from below: gpt-5.5 at xhigh (5/10 runs) and gpt-5.4 at high (5/10). gpt-5.4 at xhigh naturally reasons 600–960 tokens on this task and sailed past the 516 boundary with only one hit — consistent with a floor/threshold at the boundary rather than a general "cut everything" rule.
3. **gpt-5.4 exhibits it too.** 6/40 gpt-5.4 runs (15%) had an exact-516 event — far above the 1.3% non-gpt-5.5 base rate in the OP's aggregate. The behavior may not be 5.5-exclusive; gpt-5.5 may simply have typical reasoning lengths that sit near the first boundary more often.
4. **The only wrong answer above low effort was an exact-516 truncation.** A gpt-5.5 xhigh off run truncated at 516 answered incorrectly (the classic #29353 pattern); the other five 516-truncated off runs stayed correct — the puzzle is deliberately easy enough to grade, so it underestimates damage on genuinely hard tasks. (The one other wrong answer in the whole grid was a gpt-5.4 low run at 155 tokens — ordinary low-effort error, included as base rate.)
5. **Continuation recovers real reasoning.** Of the 5 mitigated runs that hit 516, 3 resumed with additional reasoning after replay and 2 had nothing more to add; all 5 finished correct. Mitigated conditions went 40/40 correct overall vs 38/40 unmitigated.
6. Reasoning-token distributions for on vs off are otherwise similar, so the proxy does not appear to distort baseline behavior.

**Caveats**: n=5 per cell — treat per-cell rates as coarse; the 4/5-vs-1/5 asymmetry between 5.5-xhigh off/on shares the same upstream and is plausibly sampling noise. Single puzzle, single account, single window. Happy to share the harness (prompt, runner, grader) if useful.

### Round 2: same 80-run A/B on a hard task (the community "candy" eval) — every unmitigated gpt-5.5 run was boundary-cut; accuracy 15% vs 90%

My [previous experiment](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30364#issuecomment-4892030326) used a deliberately easy puzzle; the fixed point reproduced but accuracy barely moved. This round reruns the **identical 80-run grid** (gpt-5.4/gpt-5.5 × low/medium/high/xhigh × mitigation on/off × 5 reps, interleaved, one account, one ~95-minute window, all runs exited cleanly) on a genuinely hard task: the candy pigeonhole puzzle from [haowang02/codex-candy-eval](https://github.com/haowang02/codex-candy-eval) (the community 降智 eval). Prompt verbatim from that repo, graded by its own standalone-`21` rule, `--disable memories` as in the eval. I independently verified the answer (21) by brute-force min-max before running.

\* one run's continuation stream broke and the client retried against the (cached) continued context — usage reports the retry only.

**Findings**

1. **Every single unmitigated gpt-5.5 run — 20/20, at every effort — ended its reasoning exactly on a `518·n − 2` value**: 516 ×17, plus 2588 (n=5), 4660 (n=9), 5696 (n=11). Accuracy 3/20 (15%).
2. **Which rung you land on decides the outcome.** The three correct unmitigated gpt-5.5 runs are exactly the three cut at a higher rung. Pooling both models, the split is exact: **every unmitigated run that reached ≥2588 reasoning tokens was correct (8/8); every one below that — 516-cut or naturally short — was wrong (0/32)**, including 0/22 for the 516-cut runs. The task simply needs more reasoning than 516 tokens, and the cut denies exactly that.
3. **Effort does not buy your way out.** Unmitigated gpt-5.5 at low, medium and high hit 516 in 14/15 runs; even at xhigh, 3/5 still got 516. Paying for xhigh mostly changes the *chance* of drawing a higher rung, not the cut itself.
4. **Continuation-mitigation flips accuracy from 15% to 90%** on gpt-5.5 (3/20 → 18/20; 18/20 mitigated runs triggered ≥1 continuation). Median wall time rose 26s → 86s — the continued rounds are real reasoning the model was cut off from.
5. **The rung ladder is dense and extends to at least n=21.** Across all rounds (including continuation rounds re-cut mid-fold) I observed exact terminations at n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and **21** (10876 tokens). Folds like `516 → 2588 → 2588 → clean` re-truncate on the ladder repeatedly. Four mitigated xhigh runs were cut again beyond the proxy's n≤6 detection window (e.g. `516 → continue → cut at 10876 = 518·21−2`) and still answered correctly with the extra budget.
6. **gpt-5.4 is affected too, but differently**: 5/20 unmitigated runs were 516-cut (all five wrong), yet at xhigh it usually ran 5.2–6.7k tokens with *no* cut (endings off-ladder). Whatever imposes the rungs seems to bind gpt-5.5 far more often than gpt-5.4 at the same efforts.

Three mitigated runs still failed after continuation (e.g. one 516-cut continued for only 13 further tokens and answered wrong) — continuation recovers budget, not a guarantee.

**Caveats**: n=5 per cell; one task, one account, one machine, one window (2026-07-06 19:23–20:57 UTC+8); grading is the eval's regex (a standalone "21" anywhere counts). Raw per-run data and the harness available on request.

Combined with the easy-task round (where cuts appeared only when natural reasoning length approached 516), the picture is consistent with **server-side discrete reasoning-budget rungs at 518·n − 2, with gpt-5.5 assigned the lowest rung in the vast majority of requests regardless of configured effort** — and task failure following directly from the cut.

New angle that may explain the "degraded performance on complex tasks" reports: I isolated **turn-final** responses — the last model response before the next human message, i.e. the one that produces the user-facing conclusion (completion claim, blocker declaration, validation verdict).

I regex-matched my own correction/pushback messages (challenging a false completion claim, a false "Blockers:" declaration, or an unverified validation claim) and looked up the reasoning-token count of the immediately preceding response. 28.6% of those correction moments followed a boundary-truncated response (baseline for all my messages: 21.7%) — a modest lift, but the flagship incidents (false "validation passed" claims contradicted one line later, invented blockers on credentials that existed, and losing track of the task mid-thread) each sat directly on a `reasoning_output_tokens = 516` response.

round 2: reasoning_tokens=0, shorter answer -> retried/hidden

Personally, I do not think cost optimization or automatic routing is inherently the problem.

From OpenAI's perspective, it may not be sustainable to process every request through the most expensive reasoning path all the time. If GPT-5.5 is significantly more expensive than GPT-5.4, then routing simple questions or tasks that do not require deep reasoning to a cheaper model or lower-effort path can be a reasonable product decision.

However, I think the core issue here is not whether routing exists. The issue is transparency around what the user believes they selected versus what they actually received.

If a user selects `gpt-5.5` with `xhigh` reasoning, or if the UI/CLI presents the request as being handled that way, the user will naturally expect that level of reasoning quality. But if the response repeatedly appears to stop around a specific reasoning-token boundary, such as 516, and that pattern is strongly correlated with wrong answers or shallow reasoning, users will inevitably start asking whether the selected model and effort level were really applied.

Smart routing for cost control can be reasonable. But in that case, the product should make the following clear:

- Which model and reasoning effort actually handled the request
- When and under what conditions the selected `xhigh` effort may be reduced
- What quota or cost tradeoff is required if the user wants to force deeper reasoning
- How the product communicates that a task was handled by GPT-5.4 because GPT-5.5 was not necessary

In other words, I understand that routing or reasoning-budget adjustments may be necessary as a tradeoff to avoid much higher prices. But if a user believes they are using `5.5 xhigh` while the request is silently handled through a shallower reasoning path, that looks less like cost optimization and more like a trust problem.

The best direction, in my opinion, would be transparency rather than silent limitation: default to smart routing, but allow users to explicitly force full/highest reasoning when needed, with the quota or cost impact clearly shown.

@josantonius Confirmed, and thanks for the precise repro — that was a real gap. Your read matches the code: a continuation round that answered with `reasoning_tokens=0` was classified as clean, so the fold could still deliver a 516-total response.

codexcomp v0.3.5 treats that case as a stalled nudge: after a truncation-triggered continuation, a round that comes back with zero reasoning tokens is re-nudged instead of accepted, sharing the same `--max-continue` budget (default 3). If every retry stalls, the last round's answer is still delivered — never dropped — with `proxy_stopped_reason: "max_continue"` and the per-round breakdown under `metadata.proxy_rounds`, so the outcome stays observable.

Round-1 zero-reasoning responses are deliberately untouched: a standalone response with 0 reasoning tokens can be a legitimate complete answer (your PRO run 1 without `## Intermediary updates` is an example of exactly that). The stall signal only means something after a confirmed `518n−2` truncation where the model was explicitly nudged to continue thinking.

`pip install -U codexcomp` (or `uv tool upgrade codexcomp`). If you get a chance to re-run the `--max-n 1` scenario, I'd be interested in whether the retry recovers real reasoning or exhausts the budget — `proxy_rounds` will show it either way.
